en: Not for a single moment can this Lord be absent.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Yixian of Mount Daruma in Song.
Emptiness, vastness, provisional establishment, the middle, and absolute negation—these are names for the natural essence itself.
Both are destroyed and both are established within the single Dharma-realm;
this is the natural state where names and substance are non-dual, for their substance is eternally fused. Because names do not overlap, names are eternally fixed;
emptiness manifests as vast virtue, destroying all three [realms] simultaneously. The Three Thousand Worlds and the Three Truths are like the phenomenal aspect.
Provisionally manifesting the establishment of virtue, the three [thousandfold worlds] are established together; The three thousand and the three truths are thus:
within these marks, the wondrous virtue is manifested together with the Dharma-realm. The three thousand and the three truths are thus:
the marks are the realm, and the ten suchnesses comprise the three worlds; Phenomena and principle, cause and effect, the dependent and the primary—all are fully contained therein.
The threefold perfect reality does not transcend this; it resides solely within the single thought of the ordinary.
This ultimate and exhaustive discourse on the radiance of the profound realm is inconceivable.
Taking this as the object is called the "wondrous realm"; the three thousand realms and the three truths are nothing other than this.
Taking this as contemplation is called "wondrous contemplation. Since the three thousand realms and the three truths are fundamentally no-objects, they are themselves contemplation;
thus, subject and object are forgotten. Therefore, in the initial vehicle, it is not called "contemplating objects.
How could contemplation be inconceivable? What use would there be for it? It simply requires that in a single kṣaṇa, the false and illusory be integrated.
Where the deluded mind dissolves, even truth perishes; The One Herdsman is a man who has finished his business and follows conditions as they arise.
He does not dwell upon thinking of good or evil at all; Spontaneously, evil is extinguished and goodness is formed.
In a state where there is no deliberate application of mind, vows and practices increase; With a single leap, he enters directly the ground of the Tathāgata.
It cannot be pinched into a ball, nor can it be split apart; looking and looking again, it only results in stupidity.
If one could personally reach the ground of this stupidity, the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) would originally be a source of calamity.

Ke Cha-na (Kechana) was a man who possessed both internal and external clarity, being proficient in both Chan and the Teachings; he could truly be called a renowned scholar of Kuaiji.
Ge Tian-min, whose courtesy name was Wu-huai, was the one to whom this gentleman presented the sharp-edged title "Master of Simplicity" (Pugong).
The Eizan śramaṇa Xiuyun cannot for a single moment be without this "Lord" (Cijun). The *Huayan shu* (Avataṃsaka Commentary) states:

"Prajñā can accomplish the myriad practices; what dharma is there that does not employ it? When stillness and illumination reach the ultimate limit of principle, one cannot perform even a single practice without this Lord.
Therefore, when it opens, the myriad practices flourish; when it is extinguished, they become one.

It is not that one who has attained [the Way] once would suddenly have nothing they do not understand. The *Jiaochao* says: "Regarding the phrase 'once attained' and 'one practice,' there is no such 'lord' (jun) [as a master].
This borrows terminology from non-Buddhist classics; the *Book of Jin* records that Wang Xianzhi loved bamboo so much that he planted it wherever he went.
When someone asked him the reason, he replied: "In the life of a man, one cannot for even a single day be without this lord."
The intent lies in an empty mind; one’s integrity remains unshaken through the cold of winter. Now it is clear that the myriad practices cannot for even a moment be without Prajñā.
According to the *Qingliang* [Commentary], this was an error by Wang Xianzhi; it was actually the matter of Wang Huizhi.
Huizhi was the son of Wang Yi and the elder brother of Xianzhi. The *Lìzhuan* (Biographies) volume fifty of the *Jìn Shū* (Book of Jin) states: Wang...
Wei Zhi, whose courtesy name was Ziyou, once resided in an empty dwelling and immediately ordered bamboo to be planted there.
When someone asked him the reason for this, Wei Zhi merely sighed and chanted while pointing at the bamboo, saying: "How could one be without this 'gentleman' for even a single day?

When heat exists, one should still seek refuge; when there is no sorrow, what can be forgotten? The bamboo is sparse and my body grows thin with it; the lake is near and my mind cools first.
In the victory of stillness, what need is there for chess? In this secluded clarity, no wine is required for a toast.
It is like the joy of a lingering dream: basking one's back against the morning sun.
In summer days, the morning lotus bears falling dew; The evening peaks block the slanting sun. Beneath the trees, the ground is ever shaded;
by the water’s edge, the scenery is cool. A cicada moves, startling a magpie nearby; A heron leaps, eager for its catch of fish.
Sitting alone, I observe the bustling world; In leisure, I pass the lengthening summer days.
Walking at dusk along the lake embankment, I see my reflection;
I pity the cold waters, yet what can I do about the evening sun? The heavens withhold the snow, lacking the chill.
As years approach their end, life grows longer; to whom can one entrust these fine verses? Each person in this floating world is busy with their own affairs;
having a body, I find a moment’s rest, and with nothing left to ponder, I visited Administrative Assistant Duan Shu, saying:
The waters follow the ebb of the tide; the mountains trail behind the stern. In the middle of the great river at midnight, it is full;
the double oars resound through the air. The wild geese, chilled by the cold, have not yet arrived in any number; the gulls, pure and clear, cannot find sleep.
This place, where we were teachers and friends throughout our lives— on this night, it stirs the deepest emotions.
On a snowy night, he said: "Cold blossoms reach into the secluded depths; how many more times will I visit Gushan? The cup fills all the more because of the cold;
the verse reaches its height only when it is plain. Snowdrops fall like rain from the clear eaves; pines overturn like the surging tide in the mountain ravine at night."
Though his quilt remains of iron, he still thinks of hastening to the court at dawn;
At Peian, he says:
A single path winds through pines and cypresses, Where shade forms so thickly that the sun is rarely seen; When the mountains clear, all the monks go out.
In the warm breeze, swallows fly in pairs; Fruit forms while blossoms fall from the trees. I watch idly as the mountain moon rises;
Sitting in stillness, I add another layer of clothing. The small pavilion is called: [No title provided in source]
In my small pavilion, I face the secluded thickets all day long; Sitting upright and silent, I am as if in meditative concentration.
The lush green tranquility connects with the purple bamboo of Xiang, While deep shadows cast by the verdant foliage reflect the crimson of Shu’s hibiscus.
A cat comes to playfully catch a butterfly that pierces the flowers; A sparrow descends to stealthily snatch a leaf-worm.
The slanting sun still shines upon many high willows; next year, I wish further to plant the *pīng-wáng* trees.
